question: What was our monthly revenue over the last year?
sql:
SELECT DATE_TRUNC(DATE(oi.created_at), MONTH) AS month,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders
FROM order_items oi
WHERE oi.status IN ('Complete', 'Shipped')
  AND DATE(oi.created_at) >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 12 MONTH)
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month
insight: Realised revenue counts Complete and Shipped lines only. Cancelled and Returned lines are excluded because they never became cash. We report the order count alongside revenue so a change can be attributed to volume or to basket size rather than left ambiguous.
author: analytics-team

question: Who are our top customers by total spend?
sql:
SELECT oi.user_id,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS lifetime_spend,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM order_items oi
WHERE oi.status IN ('Complete', 'Shipped')
GROUP BY oi.user_id
ORDER BY lifetime_spend DESC
LIMIT 20
insight: Rank on realised spend, never on order count: a customer with many small orders is a different commercial proposition from one with few large ones, so we return average order value in the same result to make that distinction visible. Customer identity is reported as a pseudonym.
author: analytics-team

question: Why are customers in one state spending less than another?
sql:
SELECT u.state,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS customers,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.id), 2) AS revenue_per_customer,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_item_price,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id), 2) AS items_per_order
FROM order_items oi
JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id
WHERE oi.status IN ('Complete', 'Shipped')
  AND u.state IN ('California', 'New York')
GROUP BY u.state
ORDER BY revenue_per_customer DESC
insight: An underspending question is always decomposed, never answered with one total. Revenue per customer splits into average item price times items per order; whichever of the two differs is the real finding. A state total alone confounds spend with population and is not an answer.
author: analytics-team

question: Compare the performance of two product categories and explain the difference
sql:
SELECT p.category,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_sale_price,
       ROUND(AVG(p.retail_price), 2) AS avg_list_price,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price - p.cost), 2) AS avg_margin,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.returned_at IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 4) AS return_rate
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC
insight: Category comparison needs margin and return rate beside revenue. A category can lead on revenue while losing money once returns and cost are counted, and that inversion is usually the point of the question. The gap between list price and realised sale price shows how much discounting the revenue figure required.
author: analytics-team

question: Why did our churn rate spike last month?
sql:
WITH first_order AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(DATE(created_at)) AS cohort_date
  FROM order_items
  WHERE status IN ('Complete', 'Shipped')
  GROUP BY user_id
),
monthly_active AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS active_month
  FROM order_items
  WHERE status IN ('Complete', 'Shipped')
)
SELECT DATE_TRUNC(f.cohort_date, MONTH) AS cohort_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT f.user_id) AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN m.active_month > DATE_TRUNC(f.cohort_date, MONTH)
                           THEN m.user_id END) AS returned,
       ROUND(1 - COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN m.active_month > DATE_TRUNC(f.cohort_date, MONTH)
                                     THEN m.user_id END)
                 / COUNT(DISTINCT f.user_id), 4) AS churn_rate
FROM first_order f
LEFT JOIN monthly_active m ON m.user_id = f.user_id
GROUP BY cohort_month
ORDER BY cohort_month DESC
LIMIT 18
insight: Churn is only meaningful by acquisition cohort. A month-over-month churn number moves whenever acquisition volume moves, so a spike usually reflects a large low-quality cohort acquired earlier rather than any change in customer behaviour. Always check cohort size before concluding that retention worsened.
author: analytics-team

question: Which products are underperforming relative to their list price?
sql:
SELECT p.name,
       p.category,
       p.brand,
       ROUND(p.retail_price, 2) AS list_price,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_realised,
       ROUND(1 - AVG(oi.sale_price) / NULLIF(p.retail_price, 0), 4) AS discount_depth,
       COUNT(*) AS units_sold
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.status IN ('Complete', 'Shipped')
GROUP BY p.name, p.category, p.brand, p.retail_price
HAVING units_sold >= 20
ORDER BY discount_depth DESC
LIMIT 25
insight: Underperformance means realised price well below list, not low revenue. A minimum unit threshold is essential: without it the result fills with one-off sales whose discount depth is noise rather than a pricing problem.
author: analytics-team

question: How does revenue break down by acquisition channel?
sql:
SELECT u.traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS customers,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.id), 2) AS revenue_per_customer,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.id), 2) AS orders_per_customer
FROM order_items oi
JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id
WHERE oi.status IN ('Complete', 'Shipped')
GROUP BY u.traffic_source
ORDER BY revenue DESC
insight: Channel revenue is reported per customer as well as in total, because the largest channel by volume is frequently the weakest by customer value. Acquisition decisions follow revenue per customer, not channel share.
author: analytics-team

question: What is our return rate and which categories drive it?
sql:
SELECT p.category,
       COUNT(*) AS items_sold,
       SUM(CASE WHEN oi.returned_at IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS items_returned,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.returned_at IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 4) AS return_rate,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.returned_at IS NOT NULL THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS returned_value
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category
HAVING items_sold >= 50
ORDER BY return_rate DESC
insight: Return rate is ranked alongside returned value because a high rate on a cheap category costs less than a moderate rate on an expensive one. Acting on the rate alone sends the merchandising team to the wrong category.
author: analytics-team
